posts.quote: THE GARDEN HOSE WAS THE ONLY WATER FOUNTAIN WE EVER NEEDED.
posts.caption: Nobody went inside for a drink of water. Going inside meant Mom might find you a chore, and the whole afternoon could be lost. So you grabbed the hose off the side of the house and waited for it to run cold. The first few seconds tasted like warm rubber and summer. Then it turned ice cold and you drank like a horse at a trough. You passed it to your buddy, wiped your mouth on your sleeve, and were back on your bike before the screen door could squeak.
posts.first:
Ours had a kink in it about three feet from the spigot that never came out, no matter how many times Dad straightened it. You had to hold it just right or you got nothing but a dribble. I can still taste that first warm mouthful.

posts.quote: A SPEAKER HOOKED ON THE WINDOW AND A DOUBLE FEATURE UNDER THE STARS.
posts.caption: Friday night meant the whole family piled into the car in their pajamas. Dad backed into the spot just right, hooked that heavy metal speaker on the half-rolled window, and fiddled with the volume knob. The sound was tinny and crackled every time somebody's brake lights came on. The kids were asleep in the back seat before the second picture even started. Mom always said she watched both. Nobody ever believed her.
posts.first:
We had a pink and white Ford, and Dad parked it in the same row every single time. I remember the smell of popcorn from the snack bar mixing with the bug spray Mom made us wear. I never once saw the end of the second movie.

posts.quote: YOU SAT AT THAT TABLE UNTIL YOUR PLATE WAS CLEAN. EVEN IF IT TOOK TILL BEDTIME.
posts.caption: Supper was at six, and it was not a suggestion. Whatever Mom put on that plate was what you were having, and the menu had no second page. The rest of the family would clear out, the dishes would get done, and there you sat, staring down three cold lima beans. You tried hiding them under the mashed potatoes. You tried feeding them to the dog. The dog wouldn't eat them either, and somehow Mom always knew.
posts.first:
My nemesis was stewed tomatoes. I once sat there so long the porch light came on and my father turned on the ball game in the other room just to torture me. I still won't eat them.

posts.quote: SHEETS DRIED ON THE LINE SMELLED LIKE SUNSHINE. NO BOTTLE HAS EVER COME CLOSE.
posts.caption: Monday was wash day, and the whole backyard turned white. Grandma hung sheets on the line with a mouthful of clothespins, snapping each one tight so it wouldn't wrinkle. You were in charge of the pin bag, and you took that job seriously. When a summer breeze came through, the sheets billowed like sails and you ran between them pretending you were lost at sea. That night you climbed into bed and the pillowcase smelled like the whole afternoon. Some things you just can't buy in a store.
posts.first:
My grandmother's clothesline ran from the back porch to an old apple tree, and she had a forked wooden pole to prop up the middle. If rain clouds rolled in, every kid on the property got drafted. We could clear that line in about ninety seconds.

posts.quote: Say "I'm bored" in our house and Mom had a rake in your hands before you finished the sentence. You only said it once.
posts.first:
I made that mistake exactly one time, the summer I was ten. I spent the afternoon pulling weeds out of the cracks in the driveway with a butter knife. I was never bored again, at least not out loud.

posts.quote: A HAIRCUT WAS A DOLLAR, AND THE ADVICE CAME FREE.
posts.caption: Every other Saturday, Dad walked you down to the barbershop on Main Street. You climbed up on that board laid across the arms of the big chair and tried to sit still. The place smelled like talc and hair tonic, and the radio always had a ball game on low. The men waiting their turn settled every problem in town before noon. You walked out with a crew cut, a sucker, and more opinions than you came in with. Best dollar anybody ever spent.
posts.first:
Our barber was a man named Gus who had a straight razor he kept in a jar of blue liquid like it was a science exhibit. He always ended with a splash of something on the back of your neck that stung and smelled like Christmas. I can still smell it.

posts.quote: FOUR CHANNELS AND NO REMOTE / I WAS THE REMOTE.
posts.caption: The TV in our living room was a piece of furniture, and it had exactly four channels on a good day. When Dad wanted to see what else was on, he didn't get up. He just looked at you. You walked across the room, cranked the big dial with a clunk, clunk, clunk, and waited. Then you went back to fiddle with the rabbit ears because channel 9 was all snow again. Some nights you stood there holding the antenna with one arm up for the whole last quarter. That was the job, and you did it.
posts.first:
We had a big Zenith console with a dial that went clunk so loud you could hear it from the kitchen. I spent half my childhood standing next to that set holding a piece of tinfoil on the rabbit ears. My father called me his best invention.

posts.quote: MY FIRST JOB WAS A PAPER ROUTE. RAIN OR SNOW, THAT PAPER HIT THE PORCH.
posts.caption: You were up before the rest of the house, folding papers on the kitchen floor and snapping a rubber band around each one. Then you loaded the canvas bag on your handlebars and pedaled off in the dark. You knew which dog would chase you and which porch had the loose step. Rain or snow, the paper landed by the front door, because Mr. Miller would call if it didn't. On Fridays you knocked on doors to collect, and somebody always tipped you a dime. You learned more about showing up on that route than you ever did in a classroom.
posts.first:
I had seventy-two houses on my route and I could tell you every one of them by heart for years afterward. Mrs. Kowalski gave me a plate of cookies every Christmas and a quarter tip every week. I bought my first baseball glove with that money.

posts.quote: YOU COULD BUY ONE SCREW, AND THE MAN BEHIND THE COUNTER KNEW WHICH ONE YOU NEEDED.
posts.caption: You walked in with the broken part in your pocket and laid it on the counter. The fellow behind it didn't say a word. He just turned it over in his hand, walked to the back, and came out with exactly the right thing. The floors were old wood and creaked under your feet, and every drawer held something your dad might need someday. You paid four cents and walked out with a free lesson on how to fix it. That store fixed half the town and never once tried to sell you something you didn't need.
posts.first:
Our hardware store had a wall of tiny wooden drawers that went all the way to the ceiling, with a rolling ladder to reach the top ones. Dad would send me with a busted hinge pin and a nickel. I always came home with the right part and the change.

posts.quote: WHEN IT BROKE, YOU FIXED IT. / THE TV MAN MADE HOUSE CALLS AND THE SHOE MAN KNEW YOUR NAME.
posts.caption: Nothing got thrown out just because it quit working. When the picture tube went dark, you called the TV man, and he showed up at the door with a case full of glass tubes like a doctor making a house call. When your Sunday shoes wore through, they went down to the shoe man, who put new soles on and handed them back looking better than new. Toasters got rewired. Socks got darned. Lamps got new cords. We didn't call it recycling. We called it Tuesday.
posts.first:
The TV man in our town drove a little green panel truck and always let me look at the tubes glowing in the back of the set. My mother made him coffee every time. I think he came over more than the set actually needed.
